objects: SNP genotypes; disease risk; joint and marginal association
assumptions: Genome-wide association studies of complex disease with multiple possible causal effects
conclusion: Joint SNP analysis is motivated by weak effects becoming clearer and false signals weakening after accounting for other causal effects.
scope: Motivation for simultaneous rather than single-SNP analysis; no universal power guarantee.
span: The ideal analysis of a genome-wide association (GWA) study for a complex disease would involve analysing all the SNP genotypes simultaneously to find a set of SNPs most associated with disease risk. Such an analysis can improve performance over single-SNP tests, since a weak effect may be more apparent when other causal effects are already accounted for, but also because a false signal may be weakened by inclusion in the model of a stronger signal from a true causal association.

objects: k SNP covariates; n individuals; logistic regression; case-control status
conclusion: The method poses simultaneous SNP selection as variable selection in logistic regression for case-control status.
scope: The main model analysed in this paper is case-control logistic regression.
span: We exploit recent advances in stochastic search algorithms [1],[2] to develop a computationally efficient tool to simultaneously analyse k SNPs typed in n individuals for association with case-control status, where k » n. We formulate the problem as variable selection in a logistic regression analysis that includes a covariate for each SNP.

objects: individual-level genotype matrix x; response y; coefficient vector beta

objects: posterior coefficient modes; selected nonzero coefficients

conclusion: The target is posterior modes rather than the full posterior distribution, with nonzero coefficient modes identifying the selected SNP subset.
scope: Mode-based selection; posterior inclusion probabilities are not defined here.
span: Our approach is Bayesian-inspired rather than fully Bayesian, since we seek only the posterior mode(s) rather than the full posterior distribution of the regression coefficients. If the signal of association at a SNP is weak or non-existent, the posterior mode for the corresponding covariate will remain at zero.
